newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - Hungary's draft budget eyes growth, EU.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hungary's draft budget eyes growth, EU.

text.p: Hungary's budget targets for 1997 mark a move towards sustainable growth and European Monetary Union (EMU) criteria but will not immediately solve problems inherent in the economy, analysts say.
"It is a very ambitious budget and its direction is good, but I do not see yet whether it will stimulate the economy," said research economist Laszlo Csaba.

Analysts warned that a softening of Hungary's economic programme could recreate imbalances in the current account but said plans to stop the decline in real wages were welcome as low domestic demand was a barrier to growth.

The key budget figures were likely to be approved by parliament by the end of November, and the budget law, which the House began to discuss in late October, was expected to be passed by the end of the year.

Analysts said Hungary's 18-month economic programme, designed to rein in the soaring budget and current account deficits, was successful, but budget cuts and monetary restrictions led to a slump in real wages and economic growth dropped to below one percent in 1996 from 1.5 in 1995.

As part of the package, the government cut both company tax burdens and the state budget in proportion to GDP and planned to continue along the same lines in 1997, but a hoped-for surge in investments was slow in coming.

"Among 1996 economic processes, perhaps investments show the most worrying picture," the think tank Kopint-Datorg said in a recent report, suggesting investments were likely to grow by only three percent in 1996 because companies were discouraged by low domestic demand.

The key to higher investment was the level of real wages, according to Kopint-Datorg. If wages preserved their real value in 1997, investment could increase by five to six percent and the GDP would grow by two percent.

Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy, introducing the draft budget to parliament, said 1997 would be the first year for a long time where real wages could be maintained without worsening the current account.
"We expect modest economic growth, around two percent, but this can be financed and can result in faster development later," he added.
Analysts believed the two-percent GDP growth target was realistic, but some noted this was low compared with other countries in central and eastern Europe.
"This is small, it is not good that it is only this much," said Gyorgy Csaki, deputy director of World Research Institute.

But CS First Boston's Istvan Racz said higher growth rates in the Czech Republic, Poland and Slovakia, which have similar problems to Hungary, might hinder them in cutting inflation and keeping the current account deficit low.

"Hungary has managed the problems of inflation, the budget and the current account together this year, substantially improving its position as an applicant to join the EU," he said, adding that a balanced current account and low inflation would be equally important for a new EU member.

Hungary expected inflation of 22 to 24 percent in 1996, down from 28.2 in 1995, and planned to reduce it further to some 18 percent in 1997. Analysts thought this figure ambitious, with most predicting prices would rise by 19 to 21 percent next year.
They saw the government's current account deficit and budget deficit targets as more or less realistic, but both the revenue and expenditure side of the budget remained uncertain.

"The budget includes measures to increase revenues, but tax-payers may not pay so much," said Gabor Papanek of GKI Economic Reasearch Rt. "It is an even larger risk that expenditure may surge in the year up to the (1998) elections," he added.
The government planned to balance the social security budget by introducing a minimum payment for everyone, although it had promised to cut social security contributions by 1.5 percent.

Currently the social security deficit stood at more than three times the 1996 budgeted target of 17.8 billion forints ($112 million) and analysts said it was not certain the minimum contributions would ensure the forecast surplus revenue.

Csaky said the elements of EU-standard market protection and non-monetary stimulation of exports were missing from the budget, and agricultural production, which needed funds for modernisation, would remain undersubsidised compared to EU member countries.
"Once we begin membership talks with the EU in 1998, it will be very difficult to introduce such measures," he said.
However, other planned indicators of the draft budget were likely to bring the economy closer to EMU membership criteria laid down in Maastricht, analysts said.
They said Hungary had plenty of time to meet the criteria which many EU members were also still far from achieving.
"We can become a member of the monetary union by 2002 or 2003 at the earliest," Racz said.

He added that Hungary's budget deficit in proportion to GDP was targeted at 4.9 percent for 1997, still well above the three percent Maastricht requirement but very close to the deficits of several EU members.

He said Hungary's primary budget, not including debt service payments, showed a surplus and this put pressure on the government to cut inflation so as to reduce the interest obligations of the state budget.
Hungary also had an improving state debt-to-GDP ratio, which was likely to drop to 75 percent this year from some 90 percent in 1993, approaching the EU's 60 percent requirement, Racz said.
"(With 75 percent) we are already somewhere close to the EU average," he said.
However inflation and interest rates would remain far above the Maastricht criterion for several years, analysts said.
